bp: A search system normally keeps an index outside the model: when new pages, products, or papers arrive, engineers add them to the index and the searcher can consider them. Generative retrieval changes that arrangement. The model is asked to answer a query by producing a document identifier, or docID, as text. That makes retrieval feel like generation: the model must know which identifier to emit. The practical problem is freshness. A real collection does not stand still, and a system that cannot retrieve newly added documents is stale as soon as the corpus changes. This paper serves that live-search setting. It asks how to insert new documents into a generative retriever without rebuilding the whole model and without damaging its memory of older documents. The central object is the decoder, the part that turns the model's internal query state into the next docID pieces.
wh: The hard part is that the model has not merely stored documents in a separate table. It has learned a mapping from query meaning to identifier strings inside its own settings. When a new document appears, the correct docID may be absent from the habits the decoder has learned. Incremental training sounds natural: keep training the model on the new documents. But the abstract says this is expensive, resource-intensive, and prone to catastrophic forgetting, meaning the model can become better at the new material while losing its ability to retrieve older material. The paper identifies an additional obstacle for direct model editing. Many queries share overlapping retrieval results, so the changes needed for one query can look too similar to changes needed for another. If edit vectors are indistinguishable, a targeted update may not know which query-docID relation it is supposed to repair.
naive: A smart beginner would try one of two simple fixes. The first is to run more training whenever documents are added, using the new query-document pairs until the model emits the new docIDs. That fails because frequent retraining costs too much and can overwrite old retrieval behavior. The second is to edit the decoder directly: find the output connection for a new identifier and push it upward. That also fails when many queries lead to overlapping docID sets. The edit signal for one query can resemble the edit signal for another, so a crude edit may blur several mappings together instead of teaching the model a clean new association.
ap: The paper's core idea is to treat new-document integration as a small repair to the docID mapping rather than as a full retraining job. DOME, short for docID-oriented model editing, tries to change the places in the model that matter for turning hidden states into the right new identifiers. It has three named stages: identify critical layers, optimize edit vectors, then construct and apply updates. The important move is not simply editing weights; it is making the edit vectors distinguishable enough to be useful. DOME does this with hybrid-label adaptive training. Soft labels carry query-specific meaning, so different queries that share some retrieved identifiers do not collapse into the same update. Hard labels still force the precise mapping to the correct docID. The method therefore balances two needs: preserve subtle query differences and make the new identifier output explicit.
mech: The mechanism begins with a generative retriever that already maps queries to docIDs for an original document collection. A new set of documents arrives, along with the need for the model to generate their identifiers. First, DOME searches for critical layers: the model layers whose internal states are most responsible for the decoder's ability to turn a query representation into docID outputs. This narrows the repair area so the whole model does not have to be moved. Second, it optimizes edit vectors. An edit vector is a direction of change in the model's settings: if applied, it should make a chosen hidden state point more strongly toward the correct new docID. The difficulty is that queries can share many docIDs in their retrieval results, making their desired changes look alike. DOME's hybrid-label adaptive training gives the edit process two kinds of supervision. Soft labels preserve query-specific semantics, meaning they keep graded information about which alternatives remain related to the query. Hard labels demand the exact new docID when the mapping must be corrected. Third, DOME constructs updates from those learned edit vectors and applies them to the selected layers. The output is the same kind of generative retriever, but with an updated decoder path that can produce identifiers for unseen documents while retaining effectiveness on the original collection.
math: The main mathematics is targeted error reduction. The system defines a local wrongness: for certain query states, the decoder assigns too little probability to the correct new docID. Probability here means the model's numerical belief over possible next identifier pieces. Editing asks which small change to the model's settings would reduce that wrongness without moving unrelated behavior too much. The edit vector is a direction in a high-dimensional parameter space, which can be understood as an arrow saying how to change many stored numbers together. Critical-layer identification is a selection problem: among many layers, choose the ones that most control the mapping from hidden states to docID outputs. The hybrid labels express a matching tradeoff. Hard labels make the desired answer sharp: this query should map to this identifier. Soft labels keep graded similarity among alternatives, so the model does not forget that some documents or query meanings are near each other. Optimization is the repeated adjustment of these arrows until the decoder scores the right new identifiers while old ones remain usable. The fit is natural because the practical problem is exactly a constrained mapping repair: change enough to include new documents, but not so much that the old search map is erased.
dots: This paper sits in the generative retrieval branch of information retrieval, where search becomes the act of producing identifiers rather than ranking a fixed external list. It connects to the broader ranking problem because the model still decides which document should come first; it simply expresses that decision through generated docID strings. It also connects to continual learning, the problem of learning new material without forgetting old material. Nearby repo papers make the same pressure visible from other angles: PAMT adds a memory-only stabilizing component for sequential document increments, the SID alignment work repairs stale identifiers under changing behavior, and the PAG robustness paper studies how docID generation can fail when decoding guidance drifts under query variations. DOME's specific branch is model editing. Instead of adding memory or rebuilding identifiers, it tries to surgically repair the decoder mapping for new documents.
ww: DOME should work better than naive retraining because it attacks the bottleneck named in the abstract: the decoder's mapping from hidden states to docIDs. If the model already understands much of the query language and the old collection, then the whole system does not need to be relearned just because some identifiers are new. Changing the critical layers concentrates computation where the output mapping is decided. That saves training time and reduces chances for unrelated old behavior to drift. The hybrid-label strategy addresses the main editing failure. When retrieval results overlap heavily, a pure hard target can make different edits look identical: many queries would simply say, push toward this shared set of identifiers. Soft labels preserve more of the query-specific shape, so each update can carry a finer distinction. Hard labels then anchor the final answer so the edit does not remain vague. In intuitive terms, DOME gives the repair both context and a firm destination.
po: The payoff is a more practical way to keep generative retrieval current. The abstract reports that DOME improves retrieval performance on new documents while maintaining effectiveness on the original collection. It is tested on NQ and MS MARCO, two common retrieval datasets in the repo's evidence. It also uses about 60 percent of the training time required by incremental training. That matters because document collections change repeatedly, not once. A method that can update often, spend less computation, and avoid large forgetting moves generative retrieval closer to deployment in live collections.
limits: The claims depend on the decoder bottleneck being the main failure point. If new documents require knowledge that the earlier model cannot represent in its hidden states, editing the mapping may not be enough. DOME also assumes that critical layers can be identified and that edit vectors learned from hybrid labels remain distinguishable despite overlapping retrieval results. The abstract reports effectiveness on NQ and MS MARCO, but it does not prove behavior for every corpus size, update frequency, identifier design, or adversarial document stream. It also gives training-time savings, not a full accounting of engineering cost, memory use, or long-term repeated edits.
